newsitem.title: INDIA: India industry slows down, hit by infrastructure.
newsitem.headline: India industry slows down, hit by infrastructure.

text.p: The Indian government confirmed expectations of an industrial slowdown on Friday, and analysts said manufacturing firms were being hit by low investment in infrastructure and costly credit.
The Planning Ministry reported final industrial growth figures for 1996/97 (April-March), showing overall growth of 6.7 percent, down from a handsome 11.6 percent the previous year.

"This is what we have been saying all this year. The biggest culprit in this is infrastructure," Amir Ullah Khan, an economist working for the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), told Reuters.
"What is most symptomatic is what is happening in ports. When there is all-round growth, things are lying at the berths," Khan said. "One can go on and talk about power and telecommunications."
Electricity generation grew by 3.8 percent in 1996/97, compared with 8.1 percent in 1995/96, the government said.
Industry officials expect a recovery but say it would take a few months to show up results.
"Infrastructure performance was horrible last year," said T.K. Bhaumik, senior adviser at the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII).
"If you look at the state governments, whenever there was a shortage, they imposed 100 percent power cuts," he said.
India estimates it needs nearly $80 billion worth of investment in the power sector to bridge shortfalls, and an overall $400 billion in infrastructure over the next decade.
But only a fraction of the needed investment has materialised.

Bhaumik said other factors affecting industrial growth in the fiscal year that ended last March were high interest rates and slower agricultural growth in 1995/96, which stunted disposable incomes and showed up as sluggish consumer demand the next year.
Agriculture growth dipped by 0.1 percent in 1995/96, after a rise of 4.6 percent in 1994/95. In 1996/97, it is estimated to have been around 3.7 percent.

Bhaumik said India's state-owned banks, which dominate lending to industries, were reluctant to offer credit as they were busy cleaning up their portfolios to meet tough banking standards under an economic reform programme.
"On the supply side, most of 1996/97 there was a very serious liquidity crisis. RBI (Reserve Bank of India) responded only in October 1996," he said.
Measures taken last October to ease liquidity and cut interest rates had yet to show up in industrial growth figures, he said.
On average, firms were paying interest at around 21 to 22 percent a year ago, compared with 18 to 19 at present, he added.
He also cited an overall slowdown in investment as responsible for lower industrial growth.
"There has been a decline in the capital formation. In the 1980s it was 6.5 percent (per annum). In the 1990s it is 1.5 percent," Bhaumik said. "Real investment in the economy has declined."
Besides causing infrastructure constraints, this also caused a slow growth in demand, he said.
